MOEA based memetic algorithms for multi-objective satellite range
scheduling problem
Yonghao Du a, Lining Xing a,*, Jiawei Zhang b, Yingguo Chen a, Yongming He a,c
a College of Systems Engineering, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, 410072, China
b College of Information Communication, National University of Defense Technology, Xi’an, 710106, China
c Department of Electrical & Computing Engineering, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, T6R 2V4, Canada
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Satellite range scheduling
Multi-objective optimization
Memetic algorithm
MOEA
Local search
Load-balance
A B S T R A C T
Satellite range scheduling plays a very important role in guaranteeing the normal operation and the real-time
control of in-orbit satellites. Although there appears a stronger demand for multi-objective optimization of sat-
ellite monitoring departments, multiple scheduling criteria are rarely considered simultaneously. To address the
multi-objective satellite range scheduling problem (MOSRSP), a general MOEA based memetic algorithm (MOEA-
MA) framework is proposed, which optimizes the failure rate of ground-satellite communication requests and the
load-balance degree of remote-tracking antennas. Based on a novel decision model for MOSRSP, the conﬂict-
resolution and load-balance operators and the tabu search metaheuristic are designed to implement the local
search operations in the MOEA-MA. Different types of the MOEAs, including the domination-based MOEAs,
decomposition-based MOEAs and metric-based MOEAs are adopted to implement the evolutionary operations in
the MOEA-MA. The highlight of this paper is the effective application of the MOEA-MAs to practical scheduling
problems, where the two most concerning objectives are well addressed. The MOEA-MAs that adopt ﬁve well-
known MOEAs are given and examined by the Benchmarks problems. Computational results indicate that the
MOEA-MAs outperform the original MOEAs in terms of the metrics of coverage, hypervolume and spacing, which
show good performance and application prospect for the MOSRSP.
1. Introduction
Satellites are playing an irreplaceable role in our modern lives, along
with major national projects and national defense construction. Recent
decades have witnessed wide-ranging satellite applications in remote
sensing, telecommunications, resource exploration, disaster early warn-
ing and military surveillance. All these applications need abundant and
frequent communications between satellites and ground remote-tracking
stations. These communications include but are not limited to satellite
orbit measurement, commands upload, data download and maintenance
operations, which are extremely important for the normal operation and
applications of satellites. Therefore, a type of scheduling problem called
satellite range scheduling problem (SRSP) is derived in order to ensure
the satellite-ground communication requests and to improve their
efﬁciency.
SRSP is a resource scheduling problem similar to job shop scheduling,
in which a set of ground remote-tracking resources should be assigned to
support a series of satellite-ground communication requests. But
differently, all the communications must be conducted within the
satellite-ground visible time windows, hence the SRSP is usually pro-
vided with dual constraints in resources and time. The SRSP has been
proven NP-complete [1,2] and often presents an oversubscribed char-
acter in engineering practices. For instance, in the U.S. Air Force Satellite
Control Network (AFSCN), over 300 requests were supported by only 19
antennas in a typical day in 2003 [3], and there is no successful schedule
involving all these requests until now. As early as the 1990s, Gooley [4]
has developed a mixed integer programming model to solve the SRSP
from the AFSCN. In his method, the low-altitude satellite communication
requests are ﬁrstly addressed, and then the high-altitude satellite re-
quests are scheduled as many as possible. This phased scheduling
framework is able to reduce the problem size in the SRSP and improve
the convergence speed but is inconducive to the exploration for global
optima. To address this issue, Parish [5] proposed an order-based genetic
algorithm called Genitor to globally optimize the SRSP and improved the
results from the mixed-integer programming. As illustrated in the
experimental reports of Barbulescu et al. [6,7], the Genitor also

outperforms stochastic hill-climbing, squeaky-wheel optimization and
heuristic-based stochastic sampling algorithms. So far, there appear
many other new techniques for the SRSP, such as heuristic rules [8,9],
graph colouring [10], local search metaheuristics [11,12] and evolu-
tionary algorithms [13–15]. Song et al. [16] attempted on the
multi-objective optimization for the SRSP based on the STK simulation,
where the failure rate and total proﬁt of requests are optimized,
respectively. However, these two objectives are often regarded as the
same by satellite monitoring departments since the relations between
them are noticeable. In summary, most of the previous studies made
efforts to decrease the failure rates of the requests in the SRSP under
different backgrounds and were proven effective in addressing this
objective of the SRSP.
Although the completion of satellite-ground communication requests
is particularly important, there still remain some other appealing ob-
jectives in satellite daily management. For example, the load balance
among ground remote-tracking resources, which is a different objective
from a resource view, is also a great concern for satellite monitoring
departments. The load balance makes for (1) rationalizing the utilization
of ground remote-tracking resources, (2) prolonging the resource service
lives, and (3) promoting the response capability of each resource for
emergencies; hence it is irrational to blindly pursue the completion of
requests but neglect the load balance among resources. In addition, the
existing optimization techniques for SRSP Benchmarks and engineer in-
stances could well obtain a satisfactory request failure rate around 5%
[9], so that the multi-objective optimization of other SRSP objectives
concerned by satellite monitoring departments will be much more
instructive. Therefore, the multi-objective optimization methods for
addressing different appealing objectives in the SRSP are really required.
Recent decades also witnessed the rapid development of multi-
objective optimization methods centering evolutionary algorithms, and
a large number of multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) have
been proposed [17–19]. The existing MOEAs can be divided into three
categories: (1) Domination-based MOEAs, which use the concept of
Pareto dominance to discriminate among solutions per generation. In this
type of MOEAs, non-dominated solutions in the population will be pre-
served using different strategies for the next iteration. The most popular
domination-based MOEAs include NSGA-II [20] and SPEA2 [21]. (2)
Decomposition-based MOEAs, which decompose the multi-objective
problems into several single-objective subproblems using different
weight vectors and aggregation functions. In this type of MOEAs, parent
solutions are generated from the neighboring subproblems, and the high
search performance in various problems has been demonstrated in the
literature [22–28]. (3) Metric-based MOEAs, which evaluate the perfor-
mance

Notably, although the MOEAs differ in the many aspects, the evolu-
tionary mechanisms including selections, crossovers and mutations in
these algorithms are truly similar to each other; hence the practical
multi-objective optimization problem can often be addressed by different
MOEAs. Nonetheless, the mechanisms in different MOEAs will also in-
ﬂuence the optimization effects, especially in addressing constrained and
complex

Memetic algorithms provide an idea of the combination of the
evolutionary algorithms and local search metaheuristics, and the mem-
etic algorithms that cooperate with MOEAs are getting increasingly
popular in various multi-objective optimization problems. For neural
network design, Liu et al. [34] introduced a series of adaptive
high-performance network training methods and put forward a PSO
based memetic algorithm. For wireless networks optimization problem,
Arivudainambi and Rekha [35] proposed a GA based memetic algorithm
with a r-shrink procedure. For distributed ﬂow shop scheduling prob-
lems, Deng and Wang [36] integrated several knowledge-based local
search operators into a competitive memetic algorithm and showed the
enhancement in solution exploitation. For home health care optimization
problem, Decerle et al. [38] proposed a NSGA-II based memetic algo-
rithm with the distinct individual learning provided by multi-directional
local searches. Sindhya et al. [39] pointed out the shortcomings of
MOEA/D in the convergence and introduced a gradient-based sequential
quadratic programming method to construct a hybrid MOEA/D frame-
work. Mashwani and Salhi [40] proposed a new MOEA/D based on the
PSO and differential evolution, where the PSO plays a local search engine
and differential evolution works as the main evolutionary operator.
Zhang et al. [41] embedded a gradient-based local search operator in
MOEA/D and showed its outperformance in large-scale optimization
problems. Lei et al. [42] designed a period-supplement operator and a
bi-directed local search operator with respect to examination timetabling
problems and derived the promising sets of non-dominated solutions in
their experiments. However, previous studies usually combined the local
search with one special kind of MOEA, but different MOEAs may have
their own applicable problems. As the MA centers on the combinational
idea of the MOEA and local search, other than one specially designed
algorithm, a more general MOEA based optimization framework using
the ideas of MA can be proposed and applied with different types of
MOEAs.
Inspired by the successful applications of the MOEAs and memetic
algorithms, a general MOEA based memetic algorithm (MOEA-MA)
framework is adopted in this paper for addressing the MOSRSP with the
dual objectives of the request failure rate and the load-balance degree. In
the MOEA-MA, the MOEA plays the frame algorithm, while several local
search operators are designed and triggered per generation. In each
population, evolutionary operations are implemented by crossover and
mutation operators speciﬁc to the MOSRSP, and some knowledge-based
local search operators are developed to enhance the exploitation. The
highlight of this paper is the development of a MOEA based multi-
objective memetic optimization framework for the MOSRSP. Extensive
computational experiments show that the algorithm is effective in
addressing the studied MOSRSP.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, the
MOSRSP is described and formulated. In Section 3, the framework of the
MOEA-MA is introduced and then the evolutionary and local search
operators speciﬁc to the MOSRSP are designed. Experiment setting and
computational studies are given in Section 4 and Section 5, respectively.
Finally, the paper ends with some discussions and conclusions in Section
6 and Section 7, respectively.
2. Multi-objective satellite range scheduling problem (MOSRSP)
It is obvious that the SRSP is essentially a multi-objective problem
from the previous introduction. Aiming at minimizing the objectives of
the request failure and resource load-balance degree of a given schedule,
the mathematical modeling for the MOSRSP are required. These two
objectives are not irreconcilable in satellite management, so the dual
optimization of them is reasonable and possible. In this section, several
concepts and assumptions are ﬁrst introduced, and then multi-objective
functions, as well as constraint conditions, are enumerated in the
following parts of this section.
2.1. Preliminaries
Considering that this paper focuses on the multi-objective optimiza-
tion for the MOSRSP, several reasonable assumptions are proposed to
standardize and simplify this problem referring to previous researches
and engineering experiences:

Constraint (10) implies that each request can only be executed at most
once, namely, it can only be supported by one remote-tracking antenna
within one of the visible time windows, or be cancelled. Constraint (11)
restricts that for each antenna, the time slots produced by any two
satellite-ground communications including the required turnaround time
cannot overlap, namely, the antenna can only support one communica-
tion at the same time. Notably, the constraints concerning visible time
windows, the required execution duration and the required frequency
bands are no longer formulated in this section, as they have been inte-
grated into the value ranges of the decision variable in the previous de-
cision model. In other words, the proposed decision model streamlines
the constraint conditions of the MOSRSP and reduces the decision space
of the problem naturally.
3. MOEA based memetic algorithms for MOSRSP
To resolve the multi-objective optimization of the request failure and
load-balance degree in MOSRSP, a general MOEA-MA optimization
framework and some speciﬁc evolutionary and local search meta-
heuristics are presented. In this section, the framework of the MOEA-MA
is ﬁrst introduced, and then, the encoding and decoding methods for
individuals, as well as the design of evolutionary and local search oper-
ators are illustrated in the following parts of this section.
3.1. Framework
There exist three major types of MOEAs: (1) domination-based
MOEAs, (2) decomposition-based MOEAs and (3) metric-based MOEAs.
Although these MOEAs differ in the many aspects, the evolutionary op-
erations including selections, crossovers and mutations in these algo-
rithms are truly similar. As the key idea of the MA is the combination of
the evolutionary and local search operations, these MOEAs can all well
cooperate with the local search metaheuristics for better performance.
Therefore, a memetic algorithm optimization framework regarding three
major types of MOEAs for addressing the studied MOSRSP is proposed, as
shown in Fig. 2.
(1) Regarding the domination-based MOEAs, the local search meta-
heuristics will be triggered right after the evolutionary operations
so as to strengthen the domination features of the current popu-
lation. The non-dominated sorting operations are conducted after
the combination of the parent and offspring population per gen-
eration to constitute a new offspring. The offspring of the popu-
lation will enter the next generation and play the new parents,
guiding the follow-up evolutionary operations.
(2) Regarding the decomposition-based MOEAs, for each uniformly
decomposed sub-problem, the local search operations will be
incorporated between the evolutionary operation and the refer-
ence update per generation. As the evolutionary operations will be
conducted using the neighborhood individuals of the current sub-
problems, the local search metaheuristics that work with neigh-
borhoods will be naturally appropriate and will not inﬂuence the
follow-up aggregation and the update of the decomposition-based
MOEAs.
(3) Regarding the metric-based MOEAs, with the guidance of the
metrics, the higher-metric individuals may take precedence over
non-dominated individuals; hence the local search operations
should also be guided by these metrics. In this way, the mecha-
nism that reserves higher-metric solutions per generation in this
algorithm will be facilitated. Notably, the calculation of the met-
rics should also depend on the reference surface of the problem. As
there is no theoretical or acknowledged reference surface of the
MOSRSP, the metric-based MOEAs with adaptive reference sur-
faces will be chosen in the following sections.
In addition, the possible conﬂicting set for each request will be
generated at the beginning of the MOEA-MA and used by conﬂict-
resolution operators in the incorporated local search metaheuristics.
With the help of the different operations for multi-objective optimiza-
tion, the MOEA-MA will terminate when it reaches the maximum gen-
eration and output the non-dominated solutions of the MOSRSP. Under
such circumstances, the proposed framework can be applied to all kinds
of MOEAs with different mechanisms, including the hybrid-mechanism
MOEAs such as the evolutionary many-objective optimization algo-
rithm using reference-point based non-dominated sorting approach
(NSGA-III) [32] and the evolutionary many-objective optimization al-
gorithm based on dominance and decomposition (MOEA/DD) [33].

3.3. Design of crossover and mutation operators
The two-point crossover operator is employed to perform crossover
operations in the MOSRSP, as shown in Fig. 4. (a). First, two random
break-points are used to divide the parent individuals into three seg-
ments. Secondly, both the middle segments are exchanged to generate
two offspring. In this way, the genes with respect to the same request
match up, and the value ranges for the genes are the same. On the one
hand, the genes will not exceed the value ranges or produce meaningless
solutions during the crossover operations; on the other hand, the
portioned features of the parent solutions (the supporting antennas and
time windows) will be unchanged and reserved into the offspring.

3.4. Design of local search operators
To improve the quality of iterated solutions in the MOEA-MA, three
types of local search operators and cooperated local search meta-
heuristics with the MOEA are designed. The ﬁrst operator is a conﬂict-
resolution operator, which is used to resolve the possible conﬂicts in
the individuals generated by the MOEA. The second is a load-balance
operator, which is applied to the individuals for deliberately balancing
the working-loads among the antennas. The third is a random-search
operator, which is aimed at strengthening the ability of escaping from
local optima. These three types of local search operators are devoted to
locally optimizing the population after evolutionary operations per
generation, and the descriptions on these operators are given below:

with the possible conﬂicting request set, the conﬂict-resolution operators
just alternate the genes of the possible conﬂicting requests. As shown in
Fig. 5, the conﬂict-resolution operator will randomly select one gene of
the possible conﬂicting requests, and then change the supporting antenna
of this request. For example, r1; r4 and rnr are the possible conﬂicting
requests, the operator selects the gene of r1 and changes its variable
decision from x13 ¼ 1 to x14 ¼ 1, namely, changes the supporting an-
tenna from a13 to a14. Notably, the antenna changing probability also
follows the rules of the mutation operator designed above, which aims to
ensure that this local operator will not affect the load-balance degree of
the solution too much.
(2) Load-balance operator
The load-balance operator is used to move some requests from the
high-loading antenna to low-loading antenna. For example, in Fig. 4. (b),
the 3rd antenna a13 for request r1 is the highest-loading one, while the
6th antenna a16 is lowest-loading one. Under such circumstances, the
load-balance operator is designed to mover the request r1 from the
highest-load antenna to the lowest-loading one. To avoid infeasible so-
lutions, the request can only be moved to its available antennas. In this
way, the local operator shows clear guidance in balancing the working-
load degree of the schedule and is very likely to improve the quality of
iterated solutions.
(3) Random-search operator
For the sake of the probabilistic jumping and intelligent performance,
the random searching mechanism is also required. In the MOEA-MA, the
random-search operator is designed to alternate the integer values of
genes in the individual, ranging from 0 to the number of visible time
windows for the request. The genes will be changed with a uniform
probability distribution. Although the random-search operation shows
certain blindness, it may help the algorithm escape from local optima
when the algorithm is locally trapped.
All the aforementioned local search operators will be incorporated in
a tabu search metaheuristic framework, as shown in the following
pseudo-code. It is worth mentioning that the objective function in local
search operations may be different according to the type of incorporated
MOEA. If the domination-based or decomposition-based MOEA is
incorporated (in line 6–12), the individual that dominates another will be
regarded as a better one; otherwise, when the metric-based MOEA is
incorporated (in line 13–19), the individual whose metric function M is
higher than another’s will be regarded as a better one.
Either in line 6–12 or in line 13–19, the FIFO (ﬁrst in, ﬁrst out) tabu
list LT will assist in the acceptance of individuals. Take the line 6–12 as an
example, if the obtained individual S ’ dominates the current best-found
individual S , S ’ will be accepted as the new best-found individual and
the untabued best-found individual S * regardless of the tabu list;
otherwise, when the untabued S ’ does not dominate S but dominates
S *, S ’ will also be accepted as S *, which is adopted for helping the
algorithm escape from local optima and explore a large solution space
within limited steps. In other words, the tabu list LT records the recent
individuals in this algorithm, and other untabued best-found individual
S * will be preferred to the tabued ones. Therefore, the incorporated tabu
search metaheuristic facilitates the functions of the local search. In
addition, the local search operators in the MOEA-MA also play the repair
operators. As the evolutionary operations will inevitably produce some
poor individuals in the studied constrained SRSP, the designed local
search operators can quickly obtain better individuals from their neigh-
borhoods, which well addresses the constrained optimization of the
SRSP.

4. Experiment setting
Before the computational study on the performance of the proposed
MOEA-MA framework and inner operators for addressing the MOSRSP,
the experimented scenarios and the performance metrics are introduced
ﬁrst in this section. For appropriate assignment of algorithm parameters,
the inﬂuence of parameter setting is studied then. The MOEA-MA is
programmed in the Evolutionary Multi-objective Optimization Platform
(PlatEMO) [44], which can be accessed from https://github.com/BIM
K/PlatEMO. All the algorithms are run 30 times independently using
an Intel (R) Core (TM) i7-7600U CPU at 2.80 GHz under Windows 10
with 8 GB RAM.
4.1. Experimented scenarios
The MOEA-MAs were examined on the well-known SRSP Benchmark
from AFSCN (2005), which can be accessed from http://www.cs.
colostate.edu/sched/data.html.

The Benchmark consists of seven-day satellite-ground communication
requests and involves the requests on both high-altitude satellites and
low-altitude satellites. The input of the dataset per day was the six-tuple,
which is expressed by equation (1), and a set of non-dominated solutions
using MOEA-MAs would be outputted, as well as their bi-objective
values. In the Benchmark, as the priority of each request is not given,
all the request priorities were remarked by 1. The time precision
requirement of the problem is 1 min, so the visible time windows of re-
quests given in the Benchmark were divided in minutes.

As the reference surface is unknown in the SRSPs, the AR-MOEA that

To select appropriate parameters for MOEA-MAs, the Taguchi method

there are three important parameters: (1) the crossover probability (CP),
which implies the evolutionary features of the population, (2) the mu-
tation probability (MP), which implies the diversity of the population
during the evolution, and (3) the number of local search iterations (NT),
which distinguishes MOEA-MAs from traditional MOEAs and contributes
to the solution convergence. Therefore, four levels of these three pa-

parameter setting based on an orthogonal array experiment L16(43) [36]

neighborhood exploration size for MOEA/D and MOEA/DD, and Tabu

[22].

chosen rather than the maximum number of generations as the termi-

5. Computational study
In this section, to validate the multi-objective optimization ability of
the proposed MOEA-MAs for the MOSRSP, the computational results
from different Benchmark scenarios are presented, and the algorithm
performance analysis with respect to the aforementioned metrics is
conducted. Furthermore, to distinguish the effects designed local search
operators in MOEA-MAs, some analysis on the contributions of the al-
gorithm operators is also provided.
5.1. Computational results
This subsection presents the overview of the MOEA-MAs for MOSRSP.
Seven scenarios (from SRSP1 to SRSP7) of the SRSPs in the AFSCN
Benchmark were examined. For each scenario, NSGA-II, MOEA/D, AR-
MOEA, NSGA-III and MOEA/DD and their corroding MOEA-MAs were
run 30 times to address the problem, respectively. As a result, the non-
dominated solutions obtained after a random run in different scenarios
using different algorithms are plotted in Fig. 6, where the x-axis denotes
the ﬁrst objective (the failure rate of requests) and the y-axis denotes the
second objective (the load-balance degree of antennas) of the problem.
It can be found that in most scenarios in Fig. 6, the MOEA-MAs obtain
the Pareto solutions with stronger domination than the original MOEAs.
The obtained failure rates of requests range from 0.05 to 0.35 while the
load-balance degrees of antennas range from 0.14 to 0.47. Therefore,
maintaining different levels of request failure rates, the MOEA-MAs are
able to provide many compromise solutions with various load-balance
degrees for satellite decision-makers. By comparing the Pareto fronts of
different types of algorithms, MOEA/DD and MOEA/DD-MA show good
performance in the solution spread, as the maximum-objective solutions
obtained by these two algorithms usually outperform other algorithms.
However, in contrast to other algorithms, these two algorithms seem not
to maintain the satisfactory evenness of solutions. In addition, it can also
be observed that the solutions are usually well-distributed in the x-axis,
namely the objective of the request failure rate. It is attributed to that the
failure requests are usually no many in these SRSP scenarios, the differ-
ence between the adjacent Pareto solutions in the x-axis is only one
failure request.
For a more intuitive view on the multi-objective optimization effect of
MOEA-MAs, the solutions with the highest and the lowest load-balance
degrees resulting from the MOEA/DD-MA on SRSP1 are chosen for
plotting the working time (hours) of their 19 antennas in Fig. 7 (a) and
Fig. 7 (b), respectively. The radar ﬁgure (a) indicates that for the sake of a
low request failure for satellite-ground communication, the antennas
work with quite unbalanced loads, which would cause the discontented
antenna usage in satellite monitoring departments. On the other hand,
the ﬁgure (b) shows that MOEA-MA can well address the load-balance
among the antennas and provide a very satisfactory solution for the
satellite departments, where the unbalance working loads of antenna 10,
12 and 18 are mainly due to their limited visible time windows.

6. Discussion
SRSP is a daily optimization problem faced by satellite monitoring
departments. The SRSP guarantees the normal operation and the real-
time control of in-orbit satellites, which plays an extremely important
role in satellite management. Previously, there appears a stronger de-
mand for multi-objective optimization by satellite monitoring de-
partments and many optimization techniques have been developed for
the SRSP, but multiple scheduling criteria are rarely considered simul-
taneously in existing literature. This provides a motivation for devel-
oping a multi-objective optimization method for addressing the MOSRSP
in this paper.
The main contributions of this paper are the effective MOEA-MA
framework for multi-objective optimization problems and its applica-
tion on the constrained MOSRSP. In the mathematical modeling of the
MOSRSP, two most concerned objectives, including the request failure
rate of satellite-ground communication and the load-balance degree
among remote-track antennas are addressed, and the constraints are well
streamlined by the decision model. The proposed MOEA-MA framework
is suitable for (1) domination-based MOEAs, (2) decomposition-based
MOEAs and (3) metric-based MOEAs, and the experiments using
NSGA–II–MA, MOEA/D-MA, AR-MOEA-MA, NSGA–III–MA and MOEA/
DD-MA demonstrates the effectiveness and adaptivity of the MOEA-MA.
The effectiveness and adaptivity of the MOEA-MAs should be attrib-
uted to the following three reasons: (1) The combinational idea of the
MA. With the global and diverse optimization ability from MOEAs and

problem concerning the load balance among machines and the capaci-
tated vehicle routing problem concerning the load balance among vehi-
cles. As the combinational idea of MOEAs and the local search is
applicable, as well as the conﬂict-resolution and load-balance operators
designed in this paper, the MOEA-MAs should also present satisfactory
performance. It worth mentioning that a well-designed decision model is
also required for the MOEAs on constrained scheduling problems, which
should streamline the constraint conditions and reduces the decision
space of the problem.
Despite that the two most concerned objectives of the SRSP are
involved in this paper, there still remain many other appealing factors in
satellite daily management, such as (1) the load balance among different
remote-tracking stations/regions, (2) the work concentration degree of
the antenna in a day, (3) the elevation degree of the antenna for satellite-
ground communication and (4) the communication frequency to the
same satellite. Therefore, the SRSP seems to be a many-objective opti-
mization problem, not limited to a bi-objective one. Further work con-
cerning the aforementioned objectives will be conducted and a
lightweight executable system using the MOEA-MAs will be designed. In
addition, more competitive MOEAs and local search metaheuristics will
be incorporated and studied in new MOEA-MAs.
7. Conclusion
To address the MOSRSP faced by satellite monitoring departments, a
general MOEA-MA optimization framework is proposed, which opti-
mizes the failure rate of ground-satellite communication requests and the
load-balance degree of remote-tracking antennas. A well-designed deci-
sion model for MOSRSP is also given. Different types of the MOEAs,
including the domination-based MOEAs, decomposition-based MOEAs
and metric-based MOEAs are adopted to implement the evolutionary
operations in the MOEA-MA. The MOEA-MAs that adopt ﬁve well-known
MOEAs are given and examined by the Benchmarks problems.
As the result of the application of the MOEA-MAs on Benchmarks
datasets, high-quality solutions in terms of the metrics of coverage,
hypervolume and spacing are obtained, in comparison with the original
MOEAs. The MOEA-MAs well address the MOSRSP with the two most
concerning objectives and show good adaptivity to different types of
MOEAs. In addition, it is also worthwhile to apply the MOEA-MAs on
other kinds of the resource scheduling problems with dual demands on
load balance and request proﬁts.
